# Capability example

Copy `example/` to `src/capabilities/<your-name>/`, run `npm run dev`, and reload the Chrome
extension. The build discovers `index.ts` automatically. The test harness also builds this fixture
in isolation.

Keep only the contributions and dependencies you need. When removing an index declaration, also
remove unused TypeScript files. Rename stable tool, Skill, Provider, Renderer, page, and template
IDs, along with the `example` and `example-model` message namespaces, to avoid conflicts. Import the
framework through `#sdk/*` and package files through relative `.js` paths.

| Learn how to | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Define a tool and typed results | [table-tool.ts](table-tool.ts), [result.ts](result.ts) |
| Render an interactive card and offline export | [value-card.ts](value-card.ts) |
| Add pages, settings, and draft saves | [ui.ts](ui.ts), [ui.html](ui.html), [ui.css](ui.css) |
| Translate messages and model descriptions | [messages.ts](messages.ts), [model-messages.ts](model-messages.ts) |
| Implement a local deterministic provider and authentication | [deterministic-provider.ts](deterministic-provider.ts), [presets.ts](presets.ts) |
| Supply context and observe run events | [context-and-observer.ts](context-and-observer.ts) |
| Parse documents and embed Skills | [json-document-codec.ts](json-document-codec.ts), [skills.ts](skills.ts) |

The [capability guide](../../../../src/capabilities/README.md) covers registration, SDK boundaries,
and extension development. In this example, tools and renderers share `result.ts` and parse unknown
results before displaying them. `ui.ts` uses `createSettingsForm` to separate the submitted snapshot
from later edits. Templates, images, and `srcset` use package-relative paths; styles reuse the
[design system](../../../../docs/design-system.md).

## Test the example

```bash
npm test -- playwright extension-example.spec.mjs --workers 1
npm run typecheck
```

The first command builds this fixture in isolated source and tests its tool, interactive card,
settings saves, provider, context, documents, disposal and remounting, and export. It uses synthetic
data and a local provider. Use
[extension-example.spec.mjs](../../../browser/extension-example.spec.mjs) as a starting point for
your own package's integration tests. `typecheck` checks capabilities and dependency boundaries in
the actual source tree.

## Record the demo

[`tool-renderer-example.gif`](../../../../docs/images/tool-renderer-example.gif) was recorded from
the Chrome test above using only this package's synthetic data. To record it again:

```bash
QINGZHOU_RECORD_DEMO=1 npm test -- playwright tests/browser/extension-example.spec.mjs --workers=1
```

Playwright saves `video.webm` under `tests/results/playwright/`. Convert it to a GIF at 8 fps and
760 px wide with palettegen/paletteuse. Check that the card is expanded and its result changes from
12 to 24 before replacing the public recording.

# Result selection example

Install this directory as a Skill or copy its files into a Skill created in qz. Load
`result-selection-example` and call `result_selection_example__choose` with `{"timeout":10}`.
Select one or more cards, then choose **Research selected roles**. The tool returns the selected
records to the Agent. The sample vacancies are synthetic and require no network access.

Replace the script's `items` with your collected results and keep each `id` stable. See the
[authoring guide](../../../../docs/skill-result-selection.md) for the renderer contract.

# qz

An open-source browser agent for humans and coding agents.

qz is a local-first extension for Chrome and Edge.
People use it from the side panel; agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and pi hand it web tasks
through this CLI or MCP. qz works in your own browser, with your existing logins, and returns
tables, files, or reports with sources. Everything runs locally, and your data goes only to the
model you choose.

[Website](https://alibaba.github.io/qz-browser-agent/) ·
[GitHub](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent) ·
[Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dknbdgkgoinlgjpfebapkklbmjjgdblm) ·
[Full CLI and MCP reference](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/docs/cli.md)

![A coding agent handing a GitHub research task to qz](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/main/docs/images/examples/en/pi-delegate-en.gif)

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22 or later.

1. **Install the extension.** Click **Add to Chrome** on the
   [Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dknbdgkgoinlgjpfebapkklbmjjgdblm),
   open the qz side panel, and choose a provider and model in **Settings**.
2. **Connect.** This starts the local service and pairs automatically with your default browser.

   ```bash
   npx qz-browser-agent@latest connect
   ```

3. **Run your first task.**

   ```bash
   npx qz-browser-agent@latest create "Find this year's Nobel Prize winners in every category and put them in a table with source links." --stream
   ```

   `--stream` shows progress, any questions qz needs you to answer, and the final result.

For regular use, install the `qz` command globally and use it in place of
`npx qz-browser-agent@latest`:

```bash
npm install --global qz-browser-agent@latest
qz --version
```

To let your agent learn when and how to use qz, install the Skill with
`npx skills add alibaba/qz-browser-agent -g`.

## Connect an MCP client

After `connect`, print the MCP URL:

```bash
npx qz-browser-agent@latest mcp
```

The default is `http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp`; use the URL your command prints if the port differs.

**Codex** (`~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[mcp_servers.qz]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp"
```

**Claude Code**:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http qz http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp
```

**Clients with an `mcpServers` JSON config**, such as Cursor:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "qz": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp" }
  }
}
```

CLI and MCP share the same browser connection. The MCP tool list is in the
[reference](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/docs/cli.md#task-and-resource-operations).

## Common commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `qz connect` | Start the local service and pair a browser |
| `qz status` | Check the connection and service address |
| `qz browsers` | List paired browsers, or `forget` an offline one |
| `qz create "PROMPT"` | Start a task; add `--stream` or `--wait` to follow it |
| `qz send TASK_ID "MESSAGE"` | Send a follow-up, or `--steer` the current run |
| `qz tasks` | List tasks |
| `qz show TASK_ID` | Read a task's status, response, or pending question |
| `qz watch TASK_ID` | Follow a running task until it finishes |
| `qz submit` / `approve` / `reject` | Answer a question or permission request |
| `qz cancel TASK_ID` | Stop a task |
| `qz data` | List, export, or delete data tables |
| `qz images` | List, export, or delete image collections |
| `qz skills` | Find, read, or export Skills |
| `qz settings` | Read or update settings |
| `qz automations` | List or run automations |
| `qz stop` | Stop the local service and disconnect all browsers |

With several browser profiles connected, choose one with `--client NAME|UUID` (or `-c`).
Run `qz COMMAND --help` for options. Interactive terminals show readable text; pipes receive JSON.

## Privacy and local access

The service accepts connections only on your computer, and ordinary websites cannot use its MCP
endpoint. Local programs can control connected qz tasks while the service is running. `qz stop`
disconnects all browsers and MCP clients; tasks already running in the browser keep going.
Connection settings are stored in `~/.qz-browser-agent/run/`, and pairing credentials never
leave your computer.

## Reference

See the [qz CLI and MCP reference](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/docs/cli.md)
for pairing a specific browser profile, Windows PowerShell notes, updates, task responses,
exports, output formats, exit codes, and the MCP tool mapping.

# Local conversation samples

Place qz HTML exports here to replay them with the current renderer. JSON files with a nonempty
`transcript` array are also supported; [stub.json](stub.json) shows the format. The benchmark treats
exports as recorded data and simulates Chrome APIs.

```bash
npm run benchmark -- conversation --real-examples
npm run benchmark -- conversation --real-examples --mode snapshot-render
npm run benchmark -- conversation --real-examples --mode stream-fixture-expanded
```

The runner reads `.html`, `.htm`, and `.json` files in filename order, with a fresh browser context
per sample. It skips subdirectories, symbolic links, hidden files, and `stub.json`. All samples run;
any failure or an empty corpus gives the command a failure status. Private samples are optional.

Reports default to `tests/results/conversation-real-examples/<timestamp>/`. `summary.json` records
each sample's status; `sample-N/` holds its evidence. Use `--artifact-dir` for another output root.
For single-file screenshots or baseline comparisons, pass a sample path directly.

Git tracks this README and the synthetic stub; other files and subdirectories are ignored. Keep real
conversations and their reports private, and review screenshots before sharing them.

For randomized scrolling and reading pauses, add `--stream-fuzz-seed 12345` to
`stream-fixture-interaction`. The runner checks completed tool cards each frame. Use different seeds
for repeated runs. The [test guide](../../../README.md#benchmarks-and-visual-checks) also covers
combined expansion, font-size, and viewport fuzzing. Keep its sample-path manifest in
`tests/results/`; this directory holds the conversation exports themselves.

# Privacy and browser permissions

This privacy policy covers the qz-browser-agent Chrome extension. qz stores its workspace in your
browser and connects to the model providers, websites, Skills, and MCP services you use for tasks.

## Information used by tasks

| Information | Use and destination |
| --- | --- |
| Prompts, conversations, attached files, and collected data | Stored locally; task context is sent to your configured model service to generate responses and choose actions. |
| Tab titles and URLs, page content, screenshots, and captured network data | Read for browser tasks. Tool results added to the task context are sent to the model service. Page and network content may contain personal or authentication information. |
| Bookmarks and browsing history | Read by their tools after Chrome grants access. Results used by a task are sent to the model service. |
| Location | Coordinates, accuracy, and timestamp are returned by `get_location` after first-use consent and sent to the model service for local information. |
| Model, Skill, and MCP credentials | Stored in your browser profile and used to authenticate requests to the corresponding configured services. |
| Screen recordings and exports | Created on request and saved locally. You choose whether to share the saved files. |

Skills can send task data to their configured services. Connected external agents receive tool
results and task data through MCP. Websites receive the requests, form submissions, and files
needed for the actions you request. Each receiving service applies its own privacy and retention
policy. Review those policies when choosing providers or enabling integrations.

## Storage and controls

Conversations, Skills, collections, and settings remain in your browser profile until you delete
them or clear the extension's storage. Diagnostic traces and cached resources are bounded by
storage limits. Delete chats, Skills, and collections from the side panel; remove configured
credentials in Settings. Uninstalling the extension removes its local storage. Downloaded files,
exports, and data already sent to other services are retained independently; delete those copies
at their destination.

You can stop a task, decline an access request, or disable the extension in Chrome. Chrome and your
operating system control device location access. Use HTTPS for remote model and integration
endpoints, and protect the browser profile that stores your settings and credentials.

## Limited Use

qz-browser-agent's use and transfer of information received from Chrome APIs adheres to the
[Chrome Web Store User Data Policy](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/program-policies/policies#protecting_user_privacy),
including the [Limited Use requirements](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/program-policies/limited-use).
Task data is used to provide the features you request.
qz does not sell this data or use it for advertising. Data sharing is limited to the services and
actions used to carry out your tasks, as described above.

For questions about this policy, contact the maintainers through the
[project issue tracker](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/issues). Share a description of
your question; keep credentials and personal task content out of public issues.

## Browser access

This guide explains the 19 permissions and host permission in [manifest.json](../src/manifest.json).
`history`, `bookmarks`, `desktopCapture`, and `downloads.open` are optional: Chrome requests them
when the user activates the feature. All other permissions, including `geolocation`, are declared
at installation. Chrome, operating system, and website restrictions still apply.

## Permission use

| Permission | Purpose and main callers | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sidePanel` | Open the workspace; `background/service-worker.ts` and window commands | Core UI |
| `storage` | Store model settings, Sessions, Skills, and versioned repository records | Core state |
| `unlimitedStorage` | Persist conversations, documents, Data tables, and resources locally; disk space can still run out | Core state |
| `tabs` | Read URLs, titles, and status of task-owned tabs; `background/session/tabs.ts` | Page operations |
| `tabGroups` | Group task tabs; `shared/tab-groups.ts` | Task organization |
| `scripting` | Inject Content features and self-contained functions into task pages; `background/tools/runtime.ts` | Page operations |
| `debugger` | Use CDP to operate pages, capture screenshots, inspect requests, and print PDFs; `background/tools/cdp-runtime.ts` and tools | Page operations |
| `activeTab` | Access a page after user interaction and provide a screenshot fallback for the task's target; `capabilities/media/tools.ts` | Screenshots |
| `offscreen` | Bridge sandboxed scripts, keep background work alive, and convert images; `background/services/offscreen-document.ts` | Scripts and conversion |
| `alarms` | Schedule tasks, reminders, and background maintenance; `background/automation/runtime.ts` | Scheduling |
| `downloads` | Save files, documents, and exports; file tools, Artifacts, and export features | Files |
| `downloads.open` | Open saved files from Artifacts; `capabilities/sessions/artifacts/artifacts-feature.ts` | Files |
| `desktopCapture` | Let the user choose a screen or window when recording a case; `sidepanel/features/chat/case-recording-feature.ts` | Optional recording |
| `geolocation` | Serve the `get_location` tool after first-use consent; `background/services/location.ts` | Tool request |
| `bookmarks` | Search and manage bookmarks; `capabilities/bookmarks/tools.ts` | Optional tools |
| `history` | Search browsing history; `capabilities/bookmarks/tools.ts` | Optional tools |
| `clipboardWrite` | Copy answers, code, tables, and exported page content | UI actions |
| `notifications` | Show explicit reminders and task completion notifications; `background/services/chrome-notifications.ts` | Optional notifications |
| `declarativeNetRequest` | Apply provider headers and authorized Skill network rules to extension requests; `background/services/provider-header-rules.ts`, `background/skills/skill-network.ts` | Network access |
| `<all_urls>` | Run Content Scripts, browse across sites, and access user-configured provider and Skill endpoints | Host access |

Page tools require the Session's working tab or an explicitly authorized target. Tools, navigation,
fetch, MCP, and Skill resources also enforce shared safety checks. File URLs also require Chrome's
**Allow access to file URLs** setting.

To preview a generated HTML file, query `list_downloads` with its download ID and pass the returned
`fileUrl` to `open_tab`. The URL is available once the download completes and the file still exists.
Enable **Allow access to file URLs** in the extension details at `chrome://extensions` to open,
read, or interact with it. Each task reads the setting; if disabled, its system prompt tells the
Agent to avoid local file operations. Tools check access again before operating and return
`FILE_ACCESS_REQUIRED` when disabled.

Capabilities declare operations and UI; Background and Chrome enforce access. When removing a
feature from a distribution, review its callers, stored data, authorization checks, and manifest
together.

## On-demand access

History and bookmark tools pause with an authorization card in the side panel. Clicking **Allow
and continue** opens Chrome's permission request and resumes the tool after access is granted.
This wait is outside the tool execution timeout and ends when the task is stopped. MCP callers
must complete the same authorization in the side panel.

Recording requests `desktopCapture` when the user starts recording. Opening a saved artifact
requests `downloads.open`; downloading files continues to use the required `downloads` permission.
Chrome remembers grants until the user revokes them. Subsequent use checks the current grant and
requests access again when needed.

## Denial and recovery

- Declining an optional permission cancels that action. Retry the feature to authorize it later.
- A failed `get_location` call asks the user to check device settings or provide a city or area.
- Disabled notifications make the reminder tool return `SEND_ALERT_PERMISSION_DENIED`. Completion notifications leave the task's final state intact.
- Protected pages, closed tabs, and failed CDP attachment return tool errors. Select an authorized target before retrying.
- Chrome controls screen selection. Canceling its picker ends the recording attempt.
- A failed download or file open leaves the artifact in the Session so the user can try again.
- Storage exhaustion returns a persistence failure; report a successful save after the write commits.

## First-use disclosure

The Side Panel shows a localized data disclosure before initializing the workspace. **Agree and
continue** saves the current disclosure version and opens the normal landing screen. **Maybe later**
closes the panel and leaves consent unset. The next opening shows the disclosure again.

Background gates task commands and tool execution until consent is saved. Automation scheduling,
queued follow-up recovery, and MCP bridge polling start after consent. Storage failures keep the
panel on the disclosure so users can retry. This first-use consent is separate from the location
tool's consent and Chrome's optional permission grants.

## Data flow

Requests to the selected model provider contain user input and task context, possibly after
compaction. Context can include page and file content, screenshots, tab titles and URLs, and results
from authorized bookmark and history tools. When a task needs local information, the Agent can call
`get_location`. The first call explains that coordinates, accuracy, and the location timestamp will
be sent to the configured model service. A Side Panel click records consent in local storage;
later calls reuse it. Declining leaves consent unset. Device location access and an open Side Panel
are required; a failed lookup returns recovery guidance. History and bookmarks
are read when their tools are invoked; their authorization cards explain that task results are sent
to the configured model service. Skill network access and outgoing MCP connections follow user
configuration. After first-use consent, qz enables local MCP and CLI connections. `qz connect`
starts the local service and opens a local connection page when needed. The extension verifies that
page's address and the service identity before saving its endpoint. It tries the saved endpoint
(initially `http://127.0.0.1:18765`) and becomes idle after three consecutive failures; the connection
page resumes it. Local clients can then access qz tasks and browser tools without a pairing token.
The service accepts loopback connections, validates request Host and Origin, and rejects ordinary
web-page origins. `qz stop` stops the local service. See the [connection guide](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md)
for setup and connection controls.

Provider header rules use the current `chrome.runtime.id` as their `initiatorDomains` condition.
Background installs these session rules before accepting task and model configuration commands.
Worker restarts replace the provider rules and preserve the separate Skill rule namespace.

The Chrome Web Store privacy disclosures must describe location, website content, and other task
data sent to model services, alongside any enabled Skill or MCP data flows. Keep those disclosures,
the store listing, and this policy consistent with this behavior. Use this page's public URL as the
privacy policy URL in the Chrome Web Store Developer Dashboard.

Diagnostic traces stay local. Lifecycle observers receive frozen, redacted identity and phase
metadata. Users configure model endpoints, Skill sources, and outgoing MCP connections explicitly.

For permission semantics, see the [Chrome permission
list](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/permissions-list) and [Tabs
API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/tabs). When changing the manifest,
review this table, failure paths, and packaged Chrome tests together. Moving a feature to on-demand
permissions requires request, denial, revocation, and recovery flows.

# Tests

Run tests from the repository root. Default suites use synthetic fixtures, isolated browser
profiles, and local services. See [Commands](../docs/commands.md#run-tests) for dependencies and
runner options.

## Run and filter tests

Install the locked browser binaries with `npx playwright install chromium`. Playwright and extension
tests use Chromium; standalone page fixtures also use Chromium Headless Shell. Python browser tests
use `tests/python/uv.lock` through uv. Missing dependencies fail the run.

```bash
npm test -- unit contracts
npm test -- unit --match session
npm test -- browser --list
npm test -- playwright renderer-lifecycle.spec.mjs --workers 1
npm run verify
```

| Suite | What it checks |
| --- | --- |
| `unit` | Logic, repositories, cancellation, concurrency and data formats |
| `contracts` | Side Panel projections, Port lifecycle and cross-context messages |
| `services` | Node MCP/CLI lifecycle, endpoint failures, and Agent acceptance checks |
| `browser` | Playwright, Python page smoke tests and Data Grid behavior |
| `e2e` | The loaded extension, Session exchange, documents and tool timelines |
| `release` | Deterministic builds, ZIP contents and the packaged extension |
| `visual` | Tool timelines and conversation streaming |

`npm test` selects `unit contracts services browser`; `--all` also selects E2E, release and visual.
`verify` adds type checking and coverage gates. `--list` prints the selected commands. `--match`
filters unit filenames or suite commands; the `playwright` entry accepts Playwright options
directly.

For the standalone CLI package, run `npm test -- services --match node` and
`npm test -- release --match npm-package`. The package check uses the public npm registry to
install the packed artifact in two clean temporary directories. It exercises the installed bin,
MCP handshake, tools, daemon reuse across install paths, and shutdown on a temporary port.
It uses isolated npm configuration, cache, and qz state, and cleans up its own service and files.
Use `node tests/release/npm-package.mjs --help` to retain or test a specific tarball.
The **npm package** workflow runs these checks with Node.js 22 and 24 on Linux, macOS, and Windows,
plus Node.js 22.0.0 on Linux to cover the minimum supported runtime.

The service suite checks repeated SIGINT/SIGTERM handling and listener cleanup on every platform.
On Linux and macOS it exercises the real CLI and npm's default shell during stdin input and
streaming, signaling the process group or the CLI PID and verifying that tasks and the service
remain running. Supervisors should signal their owned npm process group; delivery to the npm PID
alone depends on the shell forwarding it to the CLI.

The runner selects one to three concurrent jobs based on available CPUs. Timing-sensitive suites run
after other work. Each lane runs ready commands while dependent commands wait; build-only release
checks use the general lane. Use `npm test -- --all --jobs 1` to diagnose resource contention.
With two jobs, the auxiliary slot finishes ready general work, then runs isolated extension checks
alongside Playwright. Each extension check owns its profile; timing measurements still run alone.
`QINGZHOU_TEST_CONCURRENCY` and `QINGZHOU_PLAYWRIGHT_WORKERS` override their respective pools; suite
ownership stays in [`runner/suites.mjs`](runner/suites.mjs).

The runner uses the locked Chromium, including its full headless mode for Playwright page tests.
Native keyboard, clipboard and control fixtures retain Chromium Headless Shell.
Page tests can select `QINGZHOU_PLAYWRIGHT_CHANNEL=chrome`;
other browser entries accept `CHROME_EXECUTABLE`. Keep the browser version fixed for comparisons.

## Add a test at the right boundary

| Behavior being changed | Where to put the evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Pure logic, storage or a race | `unit/test-*.mjs`, discovered automatically |
| Client projection or message protocol | `sidepanel-rendering/`, run with `contracts` |
| Layout, focus, scrolling or user interaction | `browser/*.spec.mjs` |
| Worker restart, real Chrome storage, Port or tab ownership | `background/` extension E2E |
| A Python service | `integration/` or the service's pytest suite |
| Public TypeScript contracts | `types/`, including negative `@ts-expect-error` cases |

Test observable results and failure recovery. Session and tool changes need cancellation, obsolete
events, deletion and concurrent-write coverage where relevant. Use a loaded extension to test Worker
restart recovery. The deterministic [`background/extension-e2e.mjs`](background/extension-e2e.mjs)
provides local HTTP errors, slow streams, concurrent runs, and restart scenarios through a local
provider.

Playwright tests import `test` and `expect` from [`browser/fixtures.mjs`](browser/fixtures.mjs) to
inherit error diagnostics and coverage. Use `sidepanel-fixtures.mjs` when the full panel is needed;
its Chrome stub has explicit responses and is ready before interaction. Existing UI fixtures use
`zh-CN`; multilingual tests choose and restore their own language.

Use a small named fixture for a regression. Markdown cases live in `message-rendering/cases.js`;
formula cases and streaming checkpoints live in `mathjax/cases.js`. Tool-timeline JSON fixtures
combine `conversation.entries` with declarative `steps`; start with
[`thinking-tools-stream.json`](tool-timeline/fixtures/conversations/thinking-tools-stream.json).
Keep expected results with the test.

qz is an open-source browser agent that runs in your own browser as a Chrome extension. Describe a task in one sentence, and it works across the sites you're already signed in to, extracts the data, and delivers tables, files, or reports with sources. Connect any model, including DeepSeek, OpenAI, and Claude, with your own API key; your data stays local and goes only to the model you choose. Agents like Grok Bot, Claude Code, and Codex can also hand web tasks to qz through its CLI and MCP.

![qz collecting Hangzhou photos from Wikipedia](docs/images/workspace.png) https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/26ee85fd-540f-4427-af59-c196fadfa221 ## Why qz? ### Reliable browser execution for AI agents General-purpose AI agents often break on real-world browsing: login walls, long click sequences, and pages that load as you scroll. qz runs these flows in your real local Chrome and hands clean results back to your agent. ### Visible to you, callable by your agent Other browser agents usually let you watch them work, but stepping in mid-task is hard, and each is built for either people or agents, not both. qz lives in the side panel, so you see every step and result, and you can step in or stop it at any time. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex can also send tasks to qz through the CLI or MCP. ### Parallel research, from web data to reusable Skills qz runs many tasks at once, and each task can spawn subtasks, so a large research job is split up and worked in parallel instead of stalling a single agent. It pulls the figures you want to compare from scattered, inconsistent websites and turns them into comparison tables or local files. Once a task works, say "Save this as a Skill" and reuse it next time with one sentence. ### Your everyday browser, your data stays local No virtual environment to set up. qz uses the Chrome you already use, so your logins, cookies, and extensions just work. Task data is stored locally, and you choose the model behind it. ## What you can ask ### Start with a simple task ```text Plan a 3-day cultural walk through Luxembourg City linking the Old Town, museums, and historic quarters. Check tourism-office and venue websites for opening hours, tickets, and booking rules, build a daily route table with sources, and flag anything unverified. ```

Gathers from multiple sources and switches on Goal mode automatically.

### Pull together multiple sources ```text Compare the major open-weight LLMs released in the last 6 months, one per row: release date, parameters, context length, license, and key benchmarks, with official sources. ```

Organizes the findings into a data table.

### Get it right once, save it as a Skill in one sentence ```text Find 10 arXiv papers on browser agents from the past month, with titles, one-line takeaways, and links. ``` Once it works, say "Save this as a Skill". Next time, just say "This week's browser agent papers" to reuse it.

# Architecture

qz is a Manifest V3 Chrome extension. Background owns task state and persistence; Side Panel owns
presentation. Chrome contexts communicate through explicit protocols. The optional [MCP
bridge](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md) exposes extension operations to external clients.

For a new tool, page, renderer, provider, or embedded Skill, start with the [capability
guide](../src/capabilities/README.md). Development rules are in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md).

## Runtime map

```text
Side Panel / Chrome message / MCP
                 |
           Background API
                 |
       Session commands and supervisor
          /                    \
   Repositories              Agent
                        /             \
                 Model gateway     Tool runtime
                                       |
                           Content / Chrome / services
```

The [manifest](../src/manifest.json) declares the runtime entries.

The local CLI declares command syntax, help, and direct MCP routes in
[`commands.mjs`](../services/mcp-bridge/src/commands.mjs). A command lazily opens one MCP client and
closes it when the command finishes. CLI and MCP task observation both use
[`waitForTask`](../services/mcp-bridge/src/task-stream.mjs); it projects status, text, and actionable
input from Background snapshots. Task execution and persistence remain in the extension.

| Context | Entry and responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Background | [service-worker.ts](../src/background/service-worker.ts) composes state owners, capabilities, transports, and Chrome listeners. |
| Side Panel | [sidepanel.ts](../src/sidepanel/sidepanel.ts) initializes language; [app.ts](../src/sidepanel/app.ts) connects the workspace to Background. |
| Content | [content-script.ts](../src/content/content-script.ts) reads and operates page DOM in the isolated world. [session-export-bridge.ts](../src/content/session-export-bridge.ts) handles imports from trusted export pages. |
| Offscreen and sandbox | [offscreen.ts](../src/offscreen.ts) hosts DOM-dependent work; [runner-sandbox.ts](../src/runner-sandbox.ts) creates isolated [inner Workers](../src/workers/inner-runner.ts). |
| Local service | [MCP bridge](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md): external MCP requests and extension polling. |

[Shared](../src/shared/) defines wire/storage formats and pure transformations usable across
runtimes. [SDK modules](../src/sdk/) expose services to capabilities. Package indexes declare
contributions; generated catalogs connect them to each runtime. The [product
manifest](../src/products/manifest.json) selects adapters for the public build.

## First-use data consent

[Data consent](../src/background/services/data-consent.ts) owns the versioned acceptance record.
[Side Panel startup](../src/sidepanel/features/app/data-consent.ts) defers workspace initialization
until acceptance. The Background API gate covers transports, while Session commands guard internal
run admission. Scheduler and MCP startup wait for consent.

Location is collected by the `get_location` tool when a task needs local information. The
[location service](../src/background/services/location.ts) requests a separate first-use approval
through the Session's wait lifecycle. A Side Panel click or an explicit CLI/MCP approval of the
current disclosure version saves that approval. Continuing a task alone does not grant consent.
Approval writes recheck the pending wait and run; cancelled writes roll back before another
approval or consent read proceeds. Collection checks the run before and after asynchronous work.

## A task from submission to completion

1. A transport parses and correlates a request, then calls the
   [Background API](../src/background/background-api.ts).
2. [Session commands](../src/background/session/commands.ts) enter the supervisor's per-Session queue.
   Submission deduplicates `clientMessageId`, starts a run or queues the message, and acknowledges
   after the initial conversation write succeeds. Retries reuse the accepted message.
3. The [Agent host](../src/background/session/agent-host.ts) hydrates an
   [Agent](../src/background/agent/agent.ts) with repositories, model/tool services, and a write lease.
   Each run captures its language, tool catalogs, and [configuration](../src/background/agent/run-profile.ts).
4. The Agent gathers context, calls the model gateway, executes tools, and commits complete turns.
   Steering enters at a complete-turn boundary; queued follow-ups start subsequent runs in FIFO order.
5. [Agent events](../src/shared/contracts/agent-event.ts) pass through the host into runtime and
   transcript projections. Side Panel renders those projections.
6. `agent_end` triggers resource cleanup and terminal persistence. Notifications and observers run
   independently of that commit.

The [model gateway](../src/background/llm/index.ts) normalizes provider messages, tool calls, usage,
streaming, errors, and request admission. The Agent owns conversation history, semantic recovery,
and retry budgets. [Providers](providers.md) covers adapters, authentication, and rate policies.

[Context sources](../src/background/context-sources.ts) collect data concurrently and allocate text
budgets in registration order. Titled text becomes model context; structured results remain host
data. [Lifecycle observers](../src/background/lifecycle-observers.ts) receive identity and phase
metadata. Their `committed` phase indicates successful terminal persistence.
[Automation](../src/background/automation/runtime.ts) creates independent Sessions and reconciles
results through `automationRunId`; Chrome alarms wake the scheduler.

## Task input

[User input commands](../src/background/session/user-input.ts) expose a live wait's form and
confirmation through the Background API. CLI, MCP, and Side Panel responses use the same
validation. Each response names its Session and wait ID; stale replies leave newer waits intact.
Invalid field values keep the form pending. The supervisor settles a valid response once.
Task snapshots and rejected responses include the current input, its field IDs and option values,
and a response template bound to the wait ID. Clients can complete the next response from that
result. Templates contain defaults or placeholders; callers fill them from the user's answers.

Native Chrome permission requests remain paused until the user grants access in the Side Panel.
External approval checks the actual permission and returns `requiresUserAction` while it is absent.
The [CLI guide](cli.md#respond-to-a-task) covers input and response commands.

## Message transport

[Port transport](../src/shared/transport/port-transport.ts) sends small messages directly and
transfers large messages through a versioned chunk protocol. Callers use the same request and
response payloads.

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Chunk | 512 KiB |
| Native frame | Below 8 MiB |
| Logical message | 128 MiB |
| Encoded snapshot budget | 256 MiB; shared across Background connections |
| Receive allocation pool | 128 MiB |
| Queue per Port | 256 messages |
| Transfer deadline | 30 seconds, including capacity waits; caller deadlines also apply |

Senders encode one chunk at a time. Receivers reserve capacity before acknowledging a transfer's
start. An admitted message keeps one immutable encoded snapshot until delivery. Cancellation and
disconnect release buffers and waiting reservations; disconnect also discards incomplete transfers.

Each direction delivers complete messages in call order. Stop requests and state replies queue
behind earlier data; protocol acknowledgements and cancellation frames can pass the queue. Business
handlers run concurrently after dispatch. The client retains unsent offline messages and retires a
failed connection before handing over the next one. Accepted requests execute once.

Session imports and Skill network requests use a dedicated runtime Port with native sender
authorization and the existing operation deadlines. Request and transfer failures settle their own
requests. The event router discards replies for completed or expired requests before dispatch.
Session commands retain ownership of import, restore, save, and stop behavior.

## State, persistence, and cancellation

The [supervisor](../src/background/session/supervisor.ts) owns live Agents, epochs, runs, waits, and
write leases. The [repository](../src/background/session/repository.ts) owns records, conversations,
checkpoints, and deletion barriers. Commands coordinate them through a queue for each Session.

A lease grants write authority. `AbortSignal` requests cancellation; the host rechecks the run and
lease after asynchronous operations before accepting results. Stop establishes terminal state and
revokes subscriptions and write authority before cleanup. Delete also installs a repository
tombstone that rejects late writes. Stop preserves accepted steering and follow-ups; reset and
delete clear them. A new run receives a new epoch.

[Session codecs](../src/shared/session/session-codec.ts) normalize historical records when reading.
The repository validates record and conversation versions before selecting or replacing a copy. The
[format contract](../src/shared/session/session-format.ts) defines supported versions and errors.
List summaries and [artifact projections](../src/background/session/artifacts.ts) derive from
records, transcripts, and resource stores.

[Compaction](../src/background/agent/compaction.ts) changes the model's sending window after a
checkpoint commits. It carries earlier summaries, the Goal, and durable document references forward;
transcripts and exports retain full history. Manual and automatic compaction use this boundary.

With history trimming enabled, completed runs apply the round/token policy to old tool results and
images, protecting the latest two user rounds. While trimming is enabled, each model request also
keeps images in the latest eight image-bearing messages. Uploads and tool images share this count;
each message occupies one slot regardless of its image count. Earlier images become placeholders
while text and tool-call links remain. Sending and token estimation use the same selection. Stored
images and exports stay complete.

Resource owners check document revisions, Data versions, and Skill snapshots across asynchronous
reads and writes. Use the [Data](../src/sdk/shared/data.ts) and
[document](../src/sdk/shared/documents.ts) contracts to access those stores.

## Pages, debugger connections, and scripts

[Session tabs](../src/background/session/tabs.ts) owns the working tab and claimed tabs. Page tools
resolve targets through it. Parent and child Sessions have separate runs and tabs; creating,
claiming, and updating a tab requires the current run's authority.

[CDP runtime](../src/background/tools/cdp-runtime.ts) manages debugger connections and operation
leases. A run normally releases its connections on completion. Capabilities can retain a connection
across runs; completion or stop still revokes commands and event collection. Session deletion
releases retained connections.

[Page mode](../src/capabilities/tabs/page-mode.ts) applies mobile UA, viewport, and touch settings
before initial navigation. Mobile mode retains its connection between runs. Mode changes refresh the
page and invalidate screenshot coordinates. A lost debugger target permits one configuration
reconnect; previous page actions remain completed. User detachment ends automatic reconnection.

### Navigation readiness

`open_tab` and `navigate` share the [navigation gate](../src/capabilities/tabs/navigation.ts), using
`tabs` and `scripting`. A constant main-frame script obtains Chrome's document ID after a tab
security check. The gate waits for `pendingUrl` to clear and a new document ID to become accessible.
Fragment navigation can keep the same document.

The old-document probe has a 100 ms deadline. If it expires or fails, the fallback also requires a
`tabs.onUpdated` completion event. Polls run 50 ms apart; every awaited Chrome operation races
against cancellation. Timeout and stop release the gate and permit new-tab cleanup. New tabs are
claimed while blank, configured for mobile mode or network capture, then navigated through this
gate.

Read-only page tools also wait for an initial pending navigation to leave `about:blank`, within
their timeout and cancellation signal. They recheck access after waiting. Content injection uses
Chrome's `document_idle` timing. Dynamic page content can require an explicit element or network
wait.

### Page execution

Content returns validated [page payloads](../src/shared/contracts/page-content.ts). The [article
extractor](../src/content/article-extractor.ts) produces Markdown and preserves complex tables as
sanitized HTML. Display hints stay separate from model input.

Element actions inspect fields in Content, use CDP for text input and checkbox/radio clicks, then
read back field state. Mobile actions use touch. Optional form submission sends Enter and follows
page handlers and native validation. A CDP error ends that attempt. Multiline rich-text fields use
their paragraph writer.

[Script policy](../src/background/tools/script-policy.ts) and the [script
bridge](../src/background/tools/run-script-bridge.ts) check page and inner-script access. The inner
Worker calls tools and fetch through the host; its runtime contains only Worker APIs.

## Images and screenshots

The shared [image policy](../src/shared/images/policy.ts) and
[encoder](../src/shared/images/normalize.ts) limit images to a 2048-pixel long edge and 2 MiB
encoded. Producers normalize before sending across runtimes. Each context runs one decode/encode
operation at a time and releases the bitmap on completion, failure, or cancellation. DOM adapters
live in `src/dom/`; SVG conversion runs in offscreen and retains the original dimensions in its
result.

The model gateway limits cumulative image bytes to 48 MiB and the final adapter request to 64 MiB.
Over-budget requests return an explicit terminal error. Remote image references first pass through a
safety-checked image-reading tool. The [asset store](../src/shared/asset-store.ts) defaults to 2000
images and 1.5 GiB.

Actionable screenshots register coordinates from the final encoded dimensions. Capture reads page
identity and viewport geometry, takes the image, waits 200 ms, then compares the current state. A
changed frame triggers one retry. Requested screenshots and post-action observations use the same
path, including the retry delay. Coordinate actions require a valid screenshot. `press`, `type`, and
`scroll` use current page state; scrolling targets the viewport center.

## Tool and Skill execution

The [tool runtime](../src/background/tools/runtime.ts) checks the catalog, arguments, ownership,
safety, and rate limits before execution. It normalizes results and applies authorized effects.
Argument validation precedes target resolution. [Effect tickets](../src/background/tools/effects.ts)
come from trusted registrations. Shared [security
guards](../src/background/security-guardrails-runtime.ts) check navigation, fetch, scripts, Skills,
and MCP; user grants apply to the named target. See [permissions](permissions.md) for browser access
and recovery behavior.

[Skill tools](../src/background/skills/skill-tool-runtime.ts) use the same execution and identity
protocols. Embedded content and trusted `skillHosts` have separate contributions and validated
[provenance](../src/shared/skills/skill-provenance.ts). Installed packages execute through the
restricted Skill interfaces. [Workspace](../src/background/skills/skill-workspace.ts) writes compare
expected snapshots, prepare the registry, reconcile settings, commit, and publish in order. [Skill
network access](../src/background/skills/skill-network.ts) checks manifest permissions and shared
guards; the host injects secrets at the execution boundary.

The [MCP client](../src/background/mcp/mcp-client.ts) initializes its packaged SDK on the first
connection and reuses it for the Service Worker's lifetime. The build wraps the SDK in a cached
factory with static imports, source maps, and dependency attribution. Protocol schema initialization
runs when MCP is used.

## Side Panel projection and export

Background snapshot/event → [Session view
state](../src/sidepanel/features/sessions/session-state.ts) → [transcript
projection](../src/sidepanel/features/chat/transcript/projection.ts) → DOM reconciliation.
Connection generations, run ordering, and deletion barriers reject stale updates. [Workspace

[Presentation state](../src/sidepanel/features/chat/transcript/presentation-state.ts) owns expansion
and active-tool selection. The [renderer host](../src/sidepanel/tools/renderer-host.ts) owns

The [capability host](../src/sidepanel/capability-host/runtime.ts) registers and cleans up pages and

Heavy UI libraries load on demand and update the instance that requested them.

[Session export](../src/sidepanel/features/export/session-export-feature.ts) uses one Background

# qz CLI and MCP reference

Run browser tasks, manage results, and connect external agents to qz through CLI or MCP.
For a short overview, see the [package README](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md).
Requires Node.js 22 or later and Chrome. CLI and MCP share the same browser connection.

## Quick start

Install [qz from the Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dknbdgkgoinlgjpfebapkklbmjjgdblm)
with **Add to Chrome**. Open the qz side panel, accept the data notice shown on first use, and configure
your provider and model in Settings.

Run the published package with npx:

```bash
npx qz-browser-agent@latest connect
npx qz-browser-agent@latest create "Summarize the current page." --stream
```

`npx qz-browser-agent@latest install` opens the same Chrome Web Store page. For a manual ZIP
installation, download the [latest GitHub release](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/releases/latest)
and follow the [manual installation steps](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/README.md#manual-installation).

`connect` starts the local MCP service and pairs automatically with your default browser.
The first new profile is named `default`;
accepting the data notice alone does not enable the local connection. Repeating `connect` reuses
an online browser. Add further profiles with a [pairing URL](#pair-a-selected-browser-from-the-shell)
or from their own qz Settings.

The examples and suggested next commands use `qz`. Replace it with
`npx qz-browser-agent@latest`, or install the command globally:

```sh
npm install --global qz-browser-agent@latest
qz --version
```

On Windows, use PowerShell 7.3 or newer with its default native argument passing. After a global
install, use `qz.ps1` for commands containing JSON or quoted names; Windows command suggestions
use that wrapper. For automation, pin a compatible release version verified with your extension.

## Connect and stop

```bash
qz connect
qz status
qz browsers
qz mcp
qz stop
```

`connect` reuses the healthy service already running for this installation. It prefers port 18765;
if that port belongs to another program, the service chooses a free port. `status` shows the actual
service address, and `mcp` prints its MCP URL. Both commands are read-only. To request a custom port,
run `qz connect --port 18766`; an existing service on another port remains running and the command
reports its address. The extension connects only to its configured address.

The connection page can be closed once `qz browsers` shows the profile online. Connections start
only through `qz connect` or **qz Settings → Advanced → CLI → Connect CLI**. For ordinary connection
failures, the extension makes at most three recovery attempts, 30 seconds apart, then pauses.
After a browser or background restart, it may first wait once for the previous connection to expire.
Click **Connect CLI** in that browser's settings to retry.

To disconnect one browser, click **Disconnect: NAME** in its qz Settings. `qz stop` stops the local
service and disconnects every browser and MCP client using it. Browser tasks already running
remain in the extension; stopping the service does not cancel them. Use `qz cancel TASK_ID` to stop
a task, adding `--client NAME|UUID` when needed.

### Pair a selected browser from the shell

Get a pairing URL without opening the default browser or waiting for a connection:

```bash
qz connect --no-open --json
qz connect --no-open --name work --json
```

The JSON envelope contains `result.endpoint`, `result.url`, `result.mcpUrl`, and
`result.opened: false`. The command starts or reuses the service even when other browsers are
already connected. Open the exact returned URL in the intended browser profile with qz installed.

Set `QZ_PAIRING_URL` to that URL and `QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY` to the selected profile's directory
name, such as `Default` or `Profile 2`. These are directory names, not Chrome's display labels.
Use a profile already chosen by the user. On macOS:

```sh
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --profile-directory="$QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

For Chrome on Linux:

```sh
google-chrome --profile-directory="$QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

For Chrome installed under Program Files on Windows, set `$QzProfileDirectory` and
`$QzPairingUrl` to those same values in PowerShell:

```powershell
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" "--profile-directory=$QzProfileDirectory" $QzPairingUrl
```

Use the installed browser's executable or app name. For an existing custom data directory, also
pass `--user-data-dir` with its exact path; for example on macOS:

```sh
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --user-data-dir="$QZ_USER_DATA_DIR" --profile-directory="$QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

The [Chrome profile documentation](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/master/docs/user_data_dir.md)
distinguishes the data directory from the profile inside it. A new data directory needs its own
extension installation and first-use setup.

`--name work` adds `?name=work` to the URL. The profile opening it receives that identifier,
including when it already has a connection. Without `--name`, a registered profile keeps its name;
a new profile receives the next available name: `default`, `browser-2`, and so on. A name conflict
requires another name. `qz connect --name work` opens the URL automatically and returns immediately.
These URL-returning commands do not confirm that a browser connected. Verify it with:

```bash
qz browsers --json
qz create "Summarize the current page." --client UUID --stream
```

Read `result.browsers`, then use the intended online entry's `clientId` UUID. `--client` selects an
existing connection and cannot be combined with `--no-open` or `--name`. `--port` works with either
pairing mode and follows the existing-service behavior above.

### Add and select browsers

You can also pair from **qz Settings → Advanced → CLI** in the intended profile. Enter a distinct
browser identifier and connect. Use the service address printed by `qz status` in **Local service address** if
its port differs from 18765. Names use 1–64 letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens, beginning with
a letter or digit; names are case-sensitive. UUID-shaped names are reserved for profile IDs.

```bash
qz browsers
qz create "Summarize the current page." --client work --stream
qz show TASK_ID --client work
qz data --client work
```

`--client NAME|UUID` and `-c NAME|UUID` select a profile. With exactly one online browser, the CLI
selects it automatically. With several online browsers, a selection is required; `default` is a
name, not a routing preference. An unknown or offline selection fails without opening or using
another browser. Each command resolves its name once and carries the UUID through subsequent
requests. JSON task results and suggested next commands include that UUID.

Names remain registered while their browsers are offline and across service restarts. To release
an offline name, remove its registration explicitly:

```bash
qz browsers forget work
```

An online browser must first disconnect in its settings. Forgetting a registration leaves the
browser's tasks and data intact. A browser can then explicitly pair using the released name.

### Update the connection

Use the current CLI and extension together. Updating the npm package leaves the running service
in place; `qz status` reports an available update. Restart the connection to use the updated package:

1. Use the latest CLI and let current tasks finish.
2. Run `npx --yes qz-browser-agent@latest stop`. This disconnects all browsers using that service.
3. Update qz from the [Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dknbdgkgoinlgjpfebapkklbmjjgdblm).
   For a manual ZIP installation, replace its extracted files with the
   [latest release](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/releases/latest) and reload it at `chrome://extensions`.
4. Run `npx --yes qz-browser-agent@latest connect`, then reconnect additional profiles using their
   pairing URL or settings.

## Connect an MCP client

Run `qz connect`, then `qz mcp`. Copy the returned URL into your MCP client's HTTP configuration:

```toml
[mcp_servers.qz]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp"
```

Use the URL printed by your command if its port differs. `qz mcp --json` returns the URL as JSON
for scripts. The `qingzhou_*` MCP tool names and extension protocol remain available. Responses
to pending input bind to an explicit `waitId`. Use `qingzhou_bridge_status` to list browser names
and UUIDs, then pass `clientId: "work"` or a UUID to browser tools. Selection is required with
multiple online browsers. Task results include the resolved `clientId`. MCP initialization and streaming are handled by your
client's MCP implementation.

### Task and resource operations

CLI and MCP use the same task observer and browser operations. The task and resource commands map to these MCP operations:

| CLI | MCP tool |
| --- | --- |
| `browsers`, `browsers forget` | `qingzhou_bridge_status`, `qingzhou_forget_browser` |
| `create`, `send`, `cancel` | `qingzhou_create_session`, `qingzhou_send_message`, `qingzhou_stop_session` |
| `tasks`, `show`, `watch` | `qingzhou_list_sessions`, `qingzhou_get_session_snapshot`, `qingzhou_watch_task` |
| `show`, `submit` / `approve` / `reject` | `qingzhou_get_session_snapshot`, `qingzhou_respond_to_user_input` |
| `data list` / `delete` / `export` | `qingzhou_list_data_tables`, `qingzhou_delete_data_table`, `qingzhou_export_data_table` |
| `images list` / `delete` / `export` | `qingzhou_list_image_collections`, `qingzhou_delete_image_collection`, `qingzhou_export_image_collection` |
| `skills list` / `show` / `read` / `tools` / `export` | `qingzhou_list_skills`, `qingzhou_get_skill`, `qingzhou_get_skill_resource`, `qingzhou_list_plugins`, `qingzhou_export_skill` |
| `settings get` / `set` | `qingzhou_get_settings`, `qingzhou_update_settings` |
| `automations list` / `run` | `qingzhou_list_automations`, `qingzhou_run_automation` |

MCP creation, message submission, and input responses accept `wait: true` to wait for completion;
`stream: true` also sends assistant text through standard MCP progress notifications. A watch call
always waits. For example, call `qingzhou_create_session` with:

```json
{"firstMessage":"Summarize the current page.","stream":true}
```

Supply `_meta.progressToken` on the MCP request to receive progress. Each notification includes a
readable `message` and its structured event in `params._meta["qz/task-event"]`. Events include
`created`, `status`, `text`, `replace`, and `input`. Input events include the current form, exact
field IDs, option values, and `responseTemplate`. Fill that template and pass it to
`qingzhou_respond_to_user_input`; another CLI or MCP connection can answer while the original call
keeps waiting. Native Chrome permissions still require the user's click in the side panel.

MCP `timeoutSeconds` bounds each browser request (180 seconds by default).
`waitTimeoutSeconds` bounds the whole observation; omit it for no overall deadline. Configure your
MCP client's own request deadline for long tasks. On timeout or cancellation, the browser task
continues; error details include the task ID and a recovery tool call. `send_message` supports
`steer: true` and follows its returned `clientMessageId`, including when steering stays in the same
run. A long observation stays bound to the browser selected when it started.

When a watched task is absent from the selected browser, `task_deleted` returns a
`qingzhou_list_sessions` recovery call for that same `clientId`. Check the task ID and browser
selection before watching again. The raw snapshot tool continues to return `session: null`
for a missing task.

## Run a task

```bash
qz create "Compare these two laptops."
qz create "Summarize the current page." --title "Research" --wait
qz create "Find the main differences between these pages." --stream
qz send TASK_ID "Add the source links." --stream
qz send TASK_ID "Focus on open-source options." --steer --stream
qz tasks
qz show TASK_ID
qz cancel TASK_ID
```

`create` starts a task and returns its ID. The title is optional. `--wait` waits for the result;
`--stream` also displays progress as it arrives. Both stay connected while the task waits for user
input and continue automatically after you respond. Task observation has no default time limit.
Add `--timeout SECONDS` to set a total deadline, including time spent waiting for input. Each
individual connection request remains bounded (180 seconds by default). A timeout or Ctrl-C ends
watching; `qz watch TASK_ID --stream` resumes observation and `qz cancel TASK_ID` stops the task.

`show` returns `task_not_found` with exit code 1 when the selected browser has no matching task.
`watch` retains the `task_deleted` error code and directs you to `qz tasks --client CLIENT_UUID`.
Check the task ID and `qz browsers` before retrying; the task may have been deleted or belong to
another browser. Recovery commands keep the originally selected browser UUID.

Provide the task text directly after `create`, or read it from stdin with `qz create -`.
Use `--parent TASK_ID` to create a child task, and `qz tasks --limit N` to limit the task list.
`send TASK_ID MESSAGE` sends a follow-up to the specified task; `qz send TASK_ID -` reads the message
from stdin. A busy task queues a follow-up for its next run. Add `--steer` to deliver the message
to the current run at its next safe boundary. Both start a new run when the task is idle. Pending
questions and permissions still require a response.

`--wait` and `--stream` track the submitted message. Streaming starts after that message, including
when steering continues the same run. Pending questions from the preceding run remain visible so
you can answer them and let a queued follow-up proceed. A connection failure never resends a message
automatically.

## Respond to a task

```bash
qz show TASK_ID
qz submit TASK_ID '{"selectedIds":["option-a"]}' --stream
qz approve TASK_ID --wait
qz reject TASK_ID
qz watch TASK_ID --stream
```

`show` and pending-input notices include the current question, labeled field IDs,
option values, descriptions, image URLs, and a submission template with the actual field IDs.
Edit its placeholder values and run the displayed command to respond. `submit` takes a JSON object
keyed by field IDs; use option values for choices and arrays for multiple choices. Use
`qz submit TASK_ID -` to read answers from stdin. Invalid or stale submissions return the current
input and its template so you can correct the response directly.
`approve` continues a confirmation after you finish the requested action. `reject` declines the
current request; `cancel` stops the whole task.

Each response reads the current wait ID before sending. To answer a specific request you already
read, pass `--wait-id WAIT_ID` to `submit`, `approve`, or `reject`. A stale or invalid response
leaves the request pending. Review the application consent notice included in the pending input,
such as location sharing, before approving. Native Chrome permissions require a click in the qz side panel; CLI
approval reports that action is needed and preserves the wait without opening a browser page.
With `--wait` or `--stream`, the command stays connected while you grant permission in Chrome.
Location approval reads the current disclosure version and includes it in the response. Human
terminal output shows the notice before submitting the explicit approval; JSON output remains a
single final result. MCP callers should show the notice to the user before sending approval with
the returned `consentVersion`.

`submit`, `approve`, and `reject` accept `--wait` and `--stream` to follow the task until it finishes, including
further questions and permission requests. Each new request is shown once. Respond in the side
panel or another terminal; the original command continues automatically. `watch` follows an
existing task without resubmitting anything. Timeouts and Ctrl-C stop watching, while the task
continues in the browser.

## Browser selection and MCP tools

Use `--client NAME|UUID` or `-c NAME|UUID` to select a browser. `qz browsers` lists registered names,
UUIDs, and online status. See [browser selection](#add-and-select-browsers) for pairing and name reuse.
Use `-t` for `--title`. Run `qz help COMMAND` or `qz COMMAND --help` for command-specific options.

MCP clients can inspect browser tool schemas with `qingzhou_list_tools` and `qingzhou_get_tool`,
then call `qingzhou_execute_tool` in a task. Set `wait: false` to receive a job ID and read the result
with `qingzhou_get_tool_job`. Pass `runId` to bind execution to a particular task run. MCP also
provides `qingzhou_get_trace` and `qingzhou_clear_trace` for diagnostics.

If a request times out or its connection is interrupted, an operation already started in the
browser may still be running. Check the task before repeating it. Disconnected MCP requests are
cancelled in the service, and reconnecting does not replay their browser actions.

## Data, images, and Skills

```bash
qz data
qz data export TABLE
qz data export TABLE --format csv
qz data delete TABLE
qz images
qz images export COLLECTION
qz images delete COLLECTION
qz skills --query research
qz skills show NAME
qz skills read NAME scripts/run.js --limit 20000
qz skills tools --session TASK_ID
qz skills export NAME
```

Use the exact names printed by each list; quote names containing spaces. Data exports default to
Excel (`xlsx`); `--format csv` selects CSV. Image collections export as a ZIP containing available
image files and metadata. Missing local images are reported in the result. Skill exports contain
one user-installed Skill and its resources; built-in Skills require the extension and cannot be
exported independently.

`skills show` includes the resource paths. `skills read NAME PATH` reads one resource, with a
default limit of 20,000 characters. Use `--start` and `--limit` to select a chunk; truncated text
includes the command for the next chunk. `skills tools` lists contributed tools and whether they
are active in the selected task's context.
`skills --scope all|global|site|resident` filters by activation scope. Exports accept `--filename NAME`.
`automations --limit N` limits the automation list.

Exports use Chrome downloads. The result includes the download status, ID, filename, and path when
Chrome provides it. Check pending downloads in `chrome://downloads`. `delete` removes the named table
or image collection and its rows. Image blobs shared by other collections or task history remain
in the asset store.

## Settings and automations

```bash
qz settings
qz settings get model
qz settings set model MODEL_ID
qz settings set vision true
qz settings set '{"modelParameters":{"temperature":0.5}}'
qz settings set - < settings.json
qz automations
qz automations run AUTOMATION_ID
```

`settings` returns current values, editable fields, provider IDs, and protocol IDs. Credentials are
redacted; `qz settings get apiKey` reports whether a key is configured. `set KEY VALUE` parses JSON
values such as booleans, numbers, objects, and arrays; other values are strings. `set JSON` applies
a patch containing the supplied top-level fields. Follow the field descriptions for values that
replace an entire object, such as `modelParameters`.

Read credential patches from stdin to keep them out of shell history. JSON is validated before
connecting. The extension validates field names and values before saving. Browser commands accept
`--client NAME|UUID` to select a profile. `automations run` starts an existing automation and
returns its task ID.

The CLI uses the same browser operations as MCP. Its commands correspond to tasks, data,
images, Skills, settings, and automations. `qz mcp` only returns the connection URL for MCP
clients.

## Terminal output

Interactive terminals show readable text; pipes and redirected output receive JSON. Use `--json`
to request JSON explicitly or `--plain` to keep text when redirecting output. `--no-color` or the
`NO_COLOR` environment variable disables color. `qz mcp` prints only the MCP URL by default;
`qz mcp --json` returns a JSON result.

In JSON mode, `--wait` and `--stream` emit one final JSON result on stdout. Complete pending-input
notices and submission templates appear on stderr so you can respond while preserving
machine-readable output. MCP snapshots and rejected responses include `input`, with a
`responseTemplate` that binds answers to the current session and wait. Chrome-native permission
requests provide user instructions instead of an approval template.
Exit codes are `0` for success (including reading pending input), `1` for an operation or
task failure or a rejected submission, `2` for invalid arguments, and `130` for Ctrl-C.
Connection errors include the GitHub setup guide and installation link.

## Local access

The service accepts connections only on your computer. Ordinary websites cannot use its MCP
endpoint. Local programs can control connected qz tasks while the service is running.
Run `qz stop` to disconnect all browsers and MCP clients; existing browser tasks keep running.

Connection settings and browser registrations are stored in `~/.qz-browser-agent/run/`.
Pairing credentials stay on your computer and are omitted from status output.

Run these commands from the repository root with Node.js 24 LTS. Use `npm ci` to install the
versions in the lockfile. Build, test, and benchmark commands accept `--help`.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | Watch source files and rebuild `dist/extension/` |
| `npm run build` | Type-check and build the extension |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check TypeScript without a production build |
| `npm test` | Run unit, contract, service, and browser tests |
| `npm run verify` | Run type checking, all automated test suites, and coverage checks |
| `npm run benchmark` | Measure conversation rendering; arguments select other benchmarks |
| `npm run docs` | Generate the API reference at `dist/docs/api.md` |
| `npm run doctor` | Check the local tools, dependencies, and test browser |
| `npm run release` | Build a versioned ZIP locally |
| `npm run qz -- --help` | Show the local CLI commands for tasks, resources, and MCP |

[CLI and MCP guide](cli.md#quick-start).

## Build the extension

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
```

Load `dist/extension/` from Chrome's **Load unpacked** button. For development, run `npm run dev`
and reload the extension after each rebuild. Stop the watcher before running `build`; both use the
same output directory. If you need them at the same time, use `--output-dir` to choose another
directory. `npm run build -- --help` lists build options; `--json` emits metadata for scripts. On
failure, the last successful output stays available. A watcher owns its output until it exits; stale
locks are recovered only after confirming the owner is gone. Restart `dev` after changing build
scripts.

The public `key` in [`src/manifest.json`](../src/manifest.json) fixes the unpacked extension ID to
`ghbaodmonhcgkfeejcpffknlggbjhjgj` across checkout and installation paths. Preserve this key across
builds and releases. See Chrome's [manifest key reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/manifest/key).

## Run tests

Tests need Python 3.11+, uv, and the Chromium version installed by Playwright:

```bash
npx playwright install chromium
npm run doctor
npm test
```

On Linux, `npx playwright install-deps chromium` installs missing browser system libraries. These
tests use synthetic data and local services.

To work on one part of the project:

```bash
npm test -- unit contracts
npm test -- unit --match session
npm test -- browser --list
npm test -- playwright renderer-lifecycle.spec.mjs --workers 1
npm test -- grid
```

The suites are `unit`, `contracts`, `services`, `browser`, `e2e`, `release`, and `visual`. `--match`
filters unit filenames or suite commands. `--list` shows what would run. `browser` includes

accepts its own options.

Before submitting code changes, run `npm run verify` for the automated suites, type checks, and
coverage gates. For documentation changes, check commands, links, and examples. For narrower
coverage checks, use `npm test -- unit --coverage`. On a busy machine, `npm test -- --all --jobs 1`
runs suites sequentially.

Reports go to `tests/results/`. Use `npm test -- report` to open the Playwright report, or `npm test
-- behavior --journey H03,A07` to run the tests linked to those entries in the [behavior
index](../tests/BEHAVIOR_INDEX.md). See [tests/README.md](../tests/README.md) for details.

## Package a version

The release command builds a ZIP locally from committed Git `HEAD`:

```bash
npm run release -- --version 0.0.0.1 --summary "Local package preview"
```

Packaging installs the selected commit's locked dependencies and builds in a temporary directory. It
preserves the source manifest and writes the ZIP, README, and metadata to
`dist/releases/<version>/`. The install archive is `qz-browser-agent-extension-<version>.zip`,
with the extension under `qz-browser-agent-extension/`. The debug archive is
`qz-browser-agent-extension-<version>.debug.zip`. Distribution and Git tags are separate maintainer steps.

For a Chrome Web Store upload, select the `webstore` target:

```bash
npm run release -- --version 0.0.0.1 --target webstore
```

This writes `dist/releases/<version>/webstore/qz-browser-agent-extension-<version>.webstore.zip`
with `manifest.json` at the ZIP root. Upload this ZIP in the Chrome Developer Dashboard.
The Web Store target removes `key` from the packaged manifest. Source and manual packages retain
their public key to keep a stable extension ID during local development.
Both targets use the same runtime files. The default `manual` target keeps the installation folder;
each target has its own metadata and debug archive. The Web Store ZIP contains runtime files and
licenses; its release metadata and source maps stay alongside it. Packaging checks the single root manifest,
its referenced resources, ZIP integrity, upload size, and separation of development files.

JavaScript uses standard Terser minification, including variable shortening. `--no-minify` disables
the final Terser pass for diagnostics. Build-time script compilation retains its production settings.
Store review also covers runtime behavior, permissions, and data disclosures; this target validates
the upload package.

Use `--source worktree` to preview local edits, or `--git-ref` for another commit containing the
packaging toolchain. Scripts and dependencies come from the selected source.

Before distributing a version, obtain authorization for it, confirm the intended commit and an
unused Chrome-compatible numeric version, then run `npm ci`, `npm run doctor`, and `npm run verify`.
Package the committed source and check the output:

- `version.json` records `source: "git"` and the intended `gitCommit`.
- `target` and `packageRoot` identify the archive layout; `minification` records the Terser pass.
- Bundling and minification are enabled; runtime entries, assets, and licenses are complete.
- File counts, sizes, and SHA-256 match the package.
- The install ZIP contains compiled runtime files, licenses, and notices. Source maps are in the debug archive.

Load the ZIP's contents in an isolated Chrome profile and check the installed extension. Keep the
local `.debug.zip` with the release: it contains source maps and matching runtime hashes. Verify
those hashes before loading maps and review the source before sharing the archive.

`npm test -- release` checks deterministic output, resource integrity, obsolete-file cleanup,
license notices, and the actual minified ZIP in isolated Chrome. Fix failures with the normal
bundling and minification enabled, then rerun the affected gates. Release corrections under a new
patch version; published artifacts and tags remain immutable.

## Dependencies and static resources

Import npm dependencies from TypeScript and pin them in the root lockfile. Ordinary dependencies are
bundled with their Chrome runtime. PDF.js, MathJax and other resources loaded by URL are copied by
[vendor/assets.mjs](../scripts/vendor/assets.mjs), together with their licenses and source maps.

Each build records actual compiler inputs, including transitive dependencies, in
`vendor/provenance.json`. It contains package versions, upstream integrity and output hashes. Build
and release checks verify those hashes; copied assets and licenses must remain byte-for-byte
upstream copies. Bundling/minification only refresh provenance for compiler-owned files. Release
moves maps to the debug archive and removes their entries from installed provenance. See
[third-party notices](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

For a package published without its license text, [license
supplements](../scripts/vendor/licenses/supplements.json) pin the exact version, upstream commit and
license hash. Review the supplement again when upgrading.
